\chapter{What Passes Between Two People}
\label{ch:mr-passing-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{28}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask someone to tell me their name, quote what I said, say that I am learning Marathi, and ask whether a thing is to be had -- carrying one of the four by ear because its letter is still owed to me.}

Complete MR-R24-passing-verbs and run the exchange unaided: ask for a name with the by-ear verb, say you are learning Marathi, and ask whether water is to be had.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sāṅgṇe]{sāṅgṇe — to tell, by ear first}

\label{lesson:MR-C24-sangne}



\begin{quote}
You have asked someone's name with a whole question. There is a shorter way, and it turns on a verb you have not met.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sāṅgṇe}
\begin{quote}
\emph{sāṅgṇe} — \textbf{to tell}
\end{quote}

Asked of a person you are being polite to, it comes out \emph{sāṅgā}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{tumchaṁ nāv sāṅgā.} — \textbf{Tell me your name.}
\end{quote}

Two syllables, and it does the work your longer question was doing.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
This word is here \textbf{by ear only}, on purpose. Its middle consonant is \emph{ga} — a letter this book has shown you inside other words but has never taught your hand to make, and asking you to read a shape nobody taught you would be the one thing a gentle ramp must not do.

So carry \emph{sāṅgṇe} the way a child carries a word off a shop sign: sayable, understandable, useful today, and readable later. The letter is owed to you, and it is written down as owed.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Sāṅgṇe} comes through Prakrit \emph{saṁgai} from Sanskrit \emph{śaṃsati}, \textquotedblleft{}recites, proclaims,\textquotedblright{} on the root \emph{śaṃs-}. Behind that sits Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*\'{k}ens-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to proclaim, to declare,\textquotedblright{} which Latin took up as \emph{cēnseō}, \textquotedblleft{}I assess, I declare.\textquotedblright{} Two English words fall out of that Latin verb: \textbf{census} — the formal declaring of who lives where — and \textbf{censor}, the official who did the declaring. Telling someone your name is, at root, the same act as being counted.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sāṅgṇe} — to tell
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tumchaṁ nāv sāṅgā.} — tell me your name
  \item \emph{Run through:} \emph{basā}, then \emph{tumchaṁ nāv sāṅgā} — seat your visitor, then ask
  \item \emph{Name:} two English words on the same root — \textbf{census}, \textbf{censor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask someone to tell you their name. (\emph{Tumchaṁ nāv sāṅgā.}) What did the Sanskrit root mean? (\textbf{To recite, to proclaim}.) Why is this word not printed here in its own script? (\textbf{Its \emph{ga} has not been taught yet}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%82\%E0\%A4\%97\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: sāṅgṇe}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B6\%E0\%A4\%82\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A5\%8D}{Wiktionary: shams-}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mhaṇṇe]{\mr{म्हणणे} (mhaṇṇe) — to say these words}

\label{lesson:MR-C24-mhanne}



\begin{quote}
The last word arrived by ear alone, with one letter still owed to your hand. This one owes you nothing: every piece of it is already yours to write.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{म्हणणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{म्हणणे}} — \emph{mhaṇṇe} — \textbf{to say}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \textquotedblleft{}\mr{नमस्कार}\textquotedblright{} \mr{म्हणतो} / \mr{म्हणते}.} — \emph{mī \textquotedblleft{}namaskār\textquotedblright{} mhaṇto / mhaṇte.} — \textbf{I say \textquotedblleft{}namaskār.\textquotedblright{}}
\end{quote}

Two verbs, two jobs. \emph{Sāṅgṇe} tells a person something. \textbf{\mr{म्हणणे}} utters the words themselves — what came out of the mouth, quoted.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\mr{म}} bound to \textbf{\mr{ह}} by the halant you have written since \textbf{\mr{नमस्कार}}, then \textbf{\mr{ण}} twice, then \textbf{\mr{े}}. \textbf{\mr{म्ह}-\mr{ण}-\mr{णे}}. Say it with the breath and the \emph{m} together, not one after the other.

The same verb gives \textbf{\mr{म्हणून}} \emph{mhaṇūn}, \textquotedblleft{}therefore\textquotedblright{} — literally \emph{having said that}, which is how a good many Marathi sentences turn a corner.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{म्हणणे}} comes through Prakrit \textbf{bhaṇai} from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{भणति}} \emph{bhaṇati}, \textquotedblleft{}speaks.\textquotedblright{} The opening \textbf{\mr{भ}} \emph{bh-} did something Marathi is fond of: it shifted to the \textbf{\mr{म्ह}} \emph{mh-} cluster, breath and nasal at once. Hindi kept a plainer descendant in \emph{bhannā}. Set beside \emph{sāṅgṇe}, which came from a root for proclaiming, Marathi ended up with one verb for reciting outward and one for plain uttering.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{mhaṇṇe} — to say
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{mī \textquotedblleft{}namaskār\textquotedblright{} mhaṇto} or \textbf{mhaṇte}, whichever declares you
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{sāṅgā} and \textbf{\mr{म्हणतो}} — telling a person, uttering the words
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\mr{म्हणणे}}, and notice that every piece was already yours
  \item \emph{Read aloud:} \textbf{\mr{नमस्कार}}, whose halant and whose \textbf{\mr{र}} you are reusing here
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Sanskrit consonant became Marathi's \textbf{\mr{म्ह}}? (\textbf{\mr{भ}} \emph{bh-}.) What does \textbf{\mr{म्हणून}} mean? (\textbf{Therefore} — \textquotedblleft{}having said that\textquotedblright{}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AE\%E0\%A5\%8D\%E0\%A4\%B9\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{म्हणणे}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AD\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A4\%A4\%E0\%A4\%BF}{Wiktionary: \mr{भणति}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shikṇe]{\mr{शिकणे} (shikṇe) — to learn}

\label{lesson:MR-C24-shikne}



\begin{quote}
You can tell someone your name and you can quote what you said. The sentence a beginner most wants next is the one about what they are doing right now.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{शिकणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{शिकणे}} — \emph{shikṇe} — \textbf{to learn}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{मराठी} \mr{शिकतो} / \mr{शिकते}.} — \emph{mī marāṭhī shikto / shikte.} — \textbf{I am learning Marathi.}
\end{quote}

Said to a stranger in Maharashtra, that sentence usually ends the awkward part of the conversation and starts the good part.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\mr{श}} the \emph{sha} you write in \textbf{\mr{कशी}}, then \textbf{\mr{ि}}, then \textbf{\mr{क}}, then \textbf{\mr{णे}}. \textbf{\mr{शि}-\mr{क}-\mr{णे}}. Keep \textbf{\mr{श}} and the retroflex \textbf{\mr{ष}} apart in your ear: this word takes the softer one.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{शिकणे}} continues Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{शिक्षते}} \emph{śikṣate}, and that form is not a plain verb: it is the \textbf{desiderative} of \textbf{\mr{शक्}} \emph{śak-}, \textquotedblleft{}to be able.\textquotedblright{} A desiderative is the shape Sanskrit puts a root into to mean \emph{wanting to do it}. So \emph{to learn} was built, quite literally, as \textbf{to want to be able}.

Two familiar words fall out of the same root: \textbf{\mr{शक्ति}} \emph{śakti}, \textquotedblleft{}power, what one is able to do,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\mr{शिक्षा}} \emph{śikṣā}, \textquotedblleft{}instruction.\textquotedblright{} Every one of them is the same idea turned a different way.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{shikṇe} — to learn
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{mī marāṭhī shikto} or \textbf{shikte}, whichever declares you
  \item \emph{Say it:} what the Sanskrit root under it meant — \textbf{to be able}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{mī \textquotedblleft{}namaskār\textquotedblright{} mhaṇto}, then \textbf{mī marāṭhī shikto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say that you are learning Marathi. (\textbf{Mī marāṭhī shikto / shikte.}) What does \textbf{\mr{शक्ति}} mean, and how is it related? (\textbf{Power} — the same root, without the wanting.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B6\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{शिकणे}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B6\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A5\%8D}{Wiktionary: \mr{शक्}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[miḷṇe]{\mr{मिळणे} (miḷṇe) — to be got, to be found}

\label{lesson:MR-C24-milne}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{बरं} \mr{वाटतं}} put the feeling at you rather than in you. One more everyday verb works the same way, and it is the one you need in a shop.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{मिळणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मिळणे}} — \emph{miḷṇe} — \textbf{to be got, to be found, to be available}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{पाणी} \mr{मिळेल} \mr{का}?} — \emph{pāṇī miḷel kā?} — \textbf{Is water to be had?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{मिळतं}.} — \emph{malā miḷtaṁ.} — \textbf{I get it.}
\end{quote}

Word for word the second one is \emph{to me it is got}. English makes the person the getter; Marathi makes the thing the one that arrives. That is now the fourth sentence standing on the same dative frame.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\mr{म}}, \textbf{\mr{ि}}, then \textbf{\mr{ळ}} — the retroflex \emph{ḷ} that Hindi lost and Marathi kept, the letter inside \textbf{\mr{डोळा}} and \textbf{\mr{काळजी}} — then \textbf{\mr{णे}}. \textbf{\mr{मि}-\mr{ळ}-\mr{णे}}. Curl the tongue back for \textbf{\mr{ळ}} and let it flap.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{मिळणे}} continues Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{मिलति}} \emph{milati}, \textquotedblleft{}meets, joins, comes together.\textquotedblright{} The Sanskrit \emph{l} hardened on the way into Marathi and came out as \textbf{\mr{ळ}}. The sense travelled too: what \emph{joins} you is what you \emph{get}, so a verb about meeting became the ordinary verb for a thing being available. Hindi's \textbf{\mr{मिलना}} \emph{milnā} kept both senses side by side and kept the plain \emph{l}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{miḷṇe} — to be got
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{pāṇī miḷel kā?} — is water to be had?
  \item \emph{Run through:} the four dative sentences — \textbf{malā māhīt āhe}, \textbf{malā marāṭhī āvaḍte}, \textbf{malā baraṁ vāṭtaṁ}, \textbf{malā miḷtaṁ}
  \item \emph{Name:} the other two words you know carrying \textbf{\mr{ळ}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask whether water is to be had. (\textbf{Pāṇī miḷel kā?}) What did the Sanskrit verb behind \textbf{\mr{मिळणे}} mean? (\textbf{To meet, to join}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AE\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%B3\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{मिळणे}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AE\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%B2\%E0\%A4\%A4\%E0\%A4\%BF}{Wiktionary: \mr{मिलति}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mhaṇṇe / shikṇe / miḷṇe]{Four things that pass between two people}

\label{lesson:MR-R24-passing-verbs}



\begin{quote}
Say the four in order: \emph{sāṅgṇe}, then \textbf{\mr{म्हणणे}, \mr{शिकणे}, \mr{मिळणे}}. Three of them you can also write; one is still owed a letter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Run the three aloud, then repair only what went missing.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the four was built out of \emph{wanting to be able}? (\textbf{\mr{शिकणे}}.) Which one puts you in the dative? (\textbf{\mr{मिळणे}}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
